Paid by an owner account in this wallet: the network fee comes from that account, the payment from the Safe.
The owners’ signatures, combined into the Safe’s. Give it to the app that asked: it checks it with the Safe.
QR code of the signing request
On another phone with Freedom, the other owner scans this code from Wallet → Scan QR code. Or send the request to them with Share request.
This request is too long for a QR code: send it to the other owner with Share request, or copy it.
The shared request is the Safe’s EIP-712 typed data (eth_signTypedData_v4), so any wallet that signs typed data can sign it.
Enough owners have signed. Sending it carries out the payment from the Safe; the network fee comes from the account below.
It’s checked before it counts: it must be an owner’s signature of exactly this request.
The signatures collected here are thrown away. A signature already given to another device stays valid there until the Safe executes another transaction with this nonce.
The signatures collected here are thrown away. A signature already given to another device stays valid there for this exact message.

plurals.name: safe_discard_abandoned
plurals.item: The execution you stopped tracking (%1$s) can still be mined and make this payment: discarding doesn’t stop it. The next send from the account that paid for it reuses its nonce and replaces it.

The executions you stopped tracking (%1$s) can still be mined, and any one of them makes this payment: discarding doesn’t stop them. Sends from the account that paid for them reuse their nonces and replace them.

resources.string: This Safe isn’t active on %1$s, so who owns it can’t be checked. Freedom only co-signs for active Safes.
This isn’t a Safe signing request.
Native currency to the token contract, on top of the transfer.
A contract call: check what it does before signing.
The Safe is already past this nonce: this transaction can never execute.
The Safe’s next nonce is %1$s: earlier transactions must execute first.
Signed with %1$s. Show this to the owner collecting signatures, or copy it to them:
Freedom co-signs Safes on your networks only.
None of this wallet’s accounts owns this Safe, so it can’t sign for it.
Cancel a waiting transaction of Safe %1$s
This transaction can no longer execute, so there’s nothing to sign.
I understand this changes the Safe itself, and I trust it
It adds a new owner, who can then sign for this Safe. Together with the threshold it sets, that can give someone else control of everything in it.
It removes an owner, who can then no longer sign for this Safe, and sets how many owners must sign.
It replaces an owner with another address, which can then sign for this Safe in its place.
It changes how many owners must sign a transaction. Too low, and fewer owners — maybe one — can move everything in the Safe.
It adds a module. A module can move anything in the Safe with no owner signatures at all.
It removes a module from the Safe.
It sets the Safe’s transaction guard. A guard checks every transaction the Safe executes, and a bad one can block them all for good.
It sets the Safe’s fallback handler, which answers calls the Safe itself doesn’t know — including whether a signature is valid for it. A bad one can approve messages no owner signed.
It calls one of the Safe’s own functions that Freedom can’t read. It may change who controls the Safe.
It does nothing but use up its nonce.

The fallback handler is this Safe itself. A Safe from v1.4 on refuses that, but an older one accepts it and loses its fallback handler: it can then no longer confirm signed messages (EIP-1271) or receive NFTs sent with a safe transfer. Don’t count on this failing.
The new owner is this Safe itself, which can’t own itself: this transaction would fail.
The new owner is no address: this transaction would fail.
The new owner already owns this Safe: this transaction would fail.
The removed owner doesn’t own this Safe: this transaction would fail.
It names the wrong owner before the removed one in the Safe’s owner list: this transaction would fail.
The replaced owner doesn’t own this Safe: this transaction would fail.
It names the wrong owner before the replaced one in the Safe’s owner list: this transaction would fail.
The module is no address: this transaction would fail.
This module is already enabled on the Safe: this transaction would fail.
This module isn’t enabled on the Safe: this transaction would fail.
It names the wrong module before this one in the Safe’s module list: this transaction would fail.

This address doesn’t answer as a transaction guard right now, which a Safe from v1.4 on refuses; an older Safe doesn’t check. Its code can change before this executes too, so don’t count on this failing: a guard can block every later transaction from this Safe, including one that removes it.

resources.string: A call from the Safe to itself with no data. It only uses up Safe nonce %1$s, so no other transaction with that nonce can execute.

A call from the Safe to itself with no data, sending %2$s — more than the Safe held when it was read. Unless it holds that much when it executes it fails, and Safe nonce %1$s stays open for another transaction. Anyone can send the Safe funds before then, so don’t count on it failing either.

A call from the Safe to itself with no data: the %2$s it sends comes straight back. The Safe holds that much now, so it uses up Safe nonce %1$s and no other transaction with that nonce can execute, as long as the Safe still holds that much when it executes. If not, it fails and the nonce stays open.

A call from the Safe to itself with no data, sending %2$s straight back to it. It uses up Safe nonce %1$s only if the Safe holds that much when it executes; otherwise it fails and the nonce stays open.

When the Safe was read its next nonce was %1$s. Transactions before Safe nonce %2$s execute first and can change the Safe’s owners, so this isn’t checked against the owners it has now: don’t count on it failing, or on how many owners it leaves. Judge what it does once those have executed.

When the Safe was read its next nonce was %1$s. Transactions before Safe nonce %2$s execute first and can change the Safe’s modules, so this isn’t checked against the modules it has now: don’t count on it failing. Judge what it does once those have executed.

This Safe’s modules couldn’t all be read, and an enabled module can change the Safe’s owners at any time, with no owner signatures and no Safe nonce, so this isn’t checked against the owners it has now: don’t count on it failing, or on how many owners it leaves.

This Safe’s modules couldn’t all be read, and an enabled module can change the Safe’s modules at any time, with no owner signatures and no Safe nonce, so this isn’t checked against the modules it has now: don’t count on it failing.
